secondary_associations: The Wizard of Oz | Academy Award for Best Original Song
research_notes: Written for the 1939 MGM film The Wizard of Oz. Published 1939 by Leo Feist. Garland recorded it for the film 7 October 1938 (arrangement Murray Cutter) and commercially for Decca 28–29 July 1939. Won the Academy Award for Best Original Song. Ranked no. 1 on AFI's 100 Years…100 Songs. Year 1939 is the film/publication year.

research_notes: The theme article says John Williams composed and conducted it and that the London Symphony Orchestra recording was released as a single on 29 July 1977. The film article gives the film's country as the United States and says the score was recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra in March 1977. The soundtrack article lists Main Title as the first album track. Hedwig's Theme was already in the file, so only one further Williams title (Princess Leia's Theme) was added.

The 1977 soundtrack track list includes Princess Leia's Theme. The film article names John Williams and gives the country as the United States. Year 1977 is the soundtrack release year (June 1977) and the March 1977 recording sessions on that page. Second John Williams title in this batch; Hedwig's Theme was already present, so the three-title cap is reached.

This record is the instrumental film theme, not the later lyric version. Country pairs the American film release with the Italian composer.

secondary_associations: Spirited Away | Studio Ghibli | New Japan Philharmonic
research_notes: The music article lists あの夏へ (One Summer's Day) as track 1, composed by Joe Hisaishi, on the soundtrack released 11 July 2001, performed by the New Japan Philharmonic. It says the cue was originally instrumental and that Hisaishi later added lyrics under the title いのちの名前. Apple Music's listing dated 18 July 2001 was also returned in search; both sources agree on 2001, so the year is kept and the day is not. The film article confirms Hisaishi composed and conducted the score.

Both the music article and the film article say the closing song いつも何度でも was composed and performed by Youmi Kimura with lyrics by Wakako Kaku, and that it was written for an unproduced Miyazaki film, Rin the Chimney Painter. It is track 21 on the soundtrack released in July 2001. Not composed by Joe Hisaishi.

title_english: Rhyme from another summer: the afternoon
research_notes: The soundtrack article lists the piece, all music by Yann Tiersen, on the album released 23 April 2001. The French article calls it a solo-piano film piece by Tiersen for Jean-Pierre Jeunet's 2001 film. The composer article says the Amélie soundtrack mixed new pieces with earlier album tracks. Piano is stated on the French article.

Track 3 on the Amélie soundtrack article, music by Yann Tiersen, album released 23 April 2001. The same list also has an orchestra version and a piano version of this title; this record is the title as listed, not a separate arrangement. Second Tiersen title.

Opening track of the Amélie soundtrack article, music by Yann Tiersen, album released 23 April 2001. Third Tiersen title. The English gloss is a translation of the French title, not an official English title printed on that page.

secondary_associations: Dr. No | Vic Flick | John Barry (arrangement)
research_notes: The theme article says Monty Norman composed it and that it was first used in Dr. No (1962). It says John Barry arranged it and that the recording of 21 June 1962 used five saxophones, nine brass instruments, a solo guitar played by Vic Flick, and a rhythm section. Courts upheld Norman's authorship against Barry's claim; the Monty Norman article and the Dr. No soundtrack article repeat that outcome. The single is credited to John Barry & Orchestra. Genre on the theme article includes jazz.

The theme article says Ron Grainer wrote it and Delia Derbyshire realised it at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop in 1963, with Dick Mills assisting, using tape manipulation of a plucked string, white noise and test-tone oscillators. The NFSA page identifies Grainer as an Australian composer and dates the recording 1963. The BBC page agrees on the Grainer / Derbyshire / Mills credits. Derbyshire was not given a co-composer credit. Artist here is the person who realised the recording the sources describe.

The song article, Oricon and VGMdb agree that Yōko Takahashi sang it, Hidetoshi Satō composed it, Neko Oikawa wrote the lyrics, and Toshiyuki Ōmori arranged it. Oricon and the song article date the single 25 October 1995 and tie it to the TV Tokyo anime Neon Genesis Evangelion. The English article also says Ōmori is credited as a composer alongside Satō; VGMdb lists Satō as composer and Ōmori as arranger and co-composer. Satō is stored as composer and Ōmori as arranger in the notes.

The song article says Stephen Schwartz wrote it, that Idina Menzel and Kristin Chenoweth recorded it on 10 November 2003, and that the cast album was released 16 December 2003. The musical article says Wicked's music and lyrics are by Schwartz and that the Broadway production opened at the Gershwin Theatre in October 2003 after San Francisco tryouts. Year 2003 is the cast-recording year.

The musical article lists Popular as sung by Glinda. It identifies Kristin Chenoweth as the original Broadway Glinda and Stephen Schwartz as composer and lyricist, and dates the Broadway opening to October 2003. The cast album containing the stage songs was released 16 December 2003. Second Schwartz title.

The musical article says Dancing Through Life replaced Which Way Is the Party? as Fiyero's introductory song before Broadway, and lists it among the Act I numbers. Norbert Leo Butz is named as the original Broadway Fiyero. Schwartz is the show's composer and lyricist. Third Schwartz title. Year 2003 is the Broadway production year on that page.

The 1971 film article says the film opens with Let Them Run Clumsily, music by Vladimir Shainsky to words by Alexander Timofeevsky, and gives the film's country as the Soviet Union and release date 6 June 1971. The Gena the Crocodile article calls this Gena the Crocodile's Song. The Melodiya catalogue lists a recording by vocal quartet Ulybka with those credits. Year 1971 is the film release year, not a separately stated composition year.

The theme article says Akira Ifukube wrote Godzilla (Main Theme), Japanese title ゴジラのテーマ, for the 1954 film, and dates the recording 1954. The film article gives the country as Japan and says Ifukube composed the score, including the march later called Godzilla's theme, which he had first associated with the Self-Defense Forces.

The song article says Luiz Bonfá composed it and Antônio Maria wrote the lyrics, and that it is a principal theme of the 1959 film Orfeu Negro. In the film the character Orfeu, played by Breno Mello, is dubbed by Agostinho dos Santos. Discografia Brasileira dates a João Gilberto Odeon recording 2 July 1959 and names the same authors and the film. The film article lists countries France, Brazil and Italy; the song is filed under Brazil. Year 1959 is the film and recording year.

The film article says Antônio Carlos Jobim's song A felicidade opens Orfeu Negro (1959). It does not name a lyricist in that sentence, so songwriter is left empty. The film's countries are given as France, Brazil and Italy. Year 1959 is the French release year on that page (12 June 1959).

The film article names Samba de Orfeu, with Manhã de Carnaval, as Luiz Bonfá's contribution to the 1959 film. The Bonfá article repeats that credit. Second Bonfá title. Lyricist is not named on those pages.
